== 3. d4 ==

White attacks e5 again and threatens to win the pawn. Black must deal with the threat: trade, defend, or counterattack?

=== Trade the pawn ===

If Black allows White to trade into them, dxe5, Black won't even be able to recapture using their d-pawn because it is pinned to their queen, so doing so would allow an unfavourable queen trade. 

Most straightforwardly then, Black should trade first. [[/3...exd4|'''3...exd4''']] is the exchange Philidor. This is the main line.

=== Defend the pawn ===

Black can try defending the pawn. The chief way to do so is [[/3...Nd7|'''3...Nd7''']], the Hanham variation. White usually replies 4. Bc4, targeting  the vulnerable f7 pawn and threatening a mating trap if Black continues to develop normally. No other defence is sound:

* [[/3...Bg4|'''3...Bg4''']] is a popular amateur reply, but doesn't succeed in defending the pawn. Though Black thinks to pin the knight to White's queen, after 4. dxe5 dxe5 5. Qxd8+ (trades queens and unpins the knight) Kxd8, White's knight is unpinned and can take back on e5 anyway. If 4... Bxf3 first, as in the [[wikipedia:Opera Game|Opera Game]], 5. Qxf3 dxe5 6. Bc4 and White is threatening a crushing attack on f7. But, 3...Bg4?! can be used to gambit the pawn (see below)
* [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6?!''']] (transposing into a sort of 'declined' [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]]) is unpalatable for Black. While this looks like a more natural square for the knight than d7, it can be met with either 4. e5, kicking the knight, or 4. Bb5, pinning it (as a consequence of Black having played d6 first) and transposing into a Old Steinitz Spanish, which is not a defence held in very high regard. 
* [[/3...f6|'''3...f6?''']] defends e5 with the f pawn, but gives White more time to extend their development lead and exploit the weakened kingside.

=== Counterattack ===

Or, Black can leave the pawn undefended and counterattack White's e-pawn instead. There are two approaches: 

* [[/3...Nf6|'''3...Nf6''']], the Nimzowitsch variation, plans to meet 4. dxe5 with 4...Nxe4, after which the natural looking 5. exd6? Bxd6 leads to equality for Black.
* [[/3...f5|'''3...f5?!''']] was Philidor's Romantic recommendation, with the understanding that trading a more peripheral f-pawn to eliminate the more valuable central e-pawn is surely advantageous. 
:White has their choice of captures 4. dxe5?! fxe4 (kicks knight) 5. Ng5 d5 and while the engine still favours White, the position is unusual and perilous. 4. exf5 and the pawn can be recovered by 4...Bxf5, or the knight kicked first with 4...e4. 
:However, 3...f5?! is simply too weakening. 4. Bc4 and Black is soon facing a choice of allowing a fork by Nf7 or Qh4+ and the annihilation of their kingside.

=== Gambit the pawn ===

* While [[/3...Bg4|'''3...Bg4''']] doesn't defend the e5 pawn (see above), it allows Black to gambit it and play 4...Nd7, the Albin-Blackburne gambit. Black gives up their two central pawns for one of White's central pawns and sped up development.

Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4|Scotch game]] }} == 3...Nc6 == This is an uncommon way of playing the Philidor defence, as while the knight on c6 defends the e5 pawn, it may be pinned with Bb5. This position can arise in the Scotch game if Black declines to trade on d4 by playing 3...d6 instead. White attacks e5 twice and Black appears to defend it twice. If White trades in the centre, [[/4. dxe5|'''4. dxe5?!''']] Nxe5 5. Nxe5 dxe5 6. Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black loses castling rights, but the queens are off the board and the position is close to even. [[/4. Bb5|'''4. Bb5''']], pinning the knight to the king, removes a defender of e5 first. This is a transposition into the '''Old Steintiz defence''' in the Spanish game. The Stockfish choice is [[/4. d5|'''4. d5''']] Ne7 5. c4, closing the centre while gaining time on the knight and expanding on the queenside. Various other transpositions are possible: * '''4. Nc3''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3|Three Knights Opening]]. * '''4. Bc4''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6|Semi-Italian Opening]]. * '''4. c3''' transposes to the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3|Ponziani Opening]]. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} {{ChessMid}} ==References== ===See also=== {{Wikipedia|Philidor Defence}} {{ChessFooter}}

Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7|Hanham variation]] }} == 4. Bc4 == White develops their bishop to an active square, where it targets Black's weak f7 pawn. This is a sharp position where several ordinary seeming moves become blunders, as White can take advantage of Black's comparatively passive play to extract material concessions. [[/4...Be7|'''4...Be7?''']], developing the bishop to its only available square, loses the pawn 5. dxe5, because any attempt to recapture it result in Black tactically losing a minor piece due to pressure on f7 (5...dxe5 6. Qd5! or 5...Nxe5 6. Nxe5 dxe5 7. Qh5). [[/4...Ngf6|'''4...Ngf6?''']] develops the knight and seems like an improvement, as it controls the d5 and h5 squares preventing White's queen from infiltrating. But after 5. dxe5 Black still cannot recover the pawn: * 5...dxe5 allows 6. Ng5! (without ...Be7 g5 is unguarded) and Black has to give up at least a piece to prevent Bxf7 Ke7 Ne7!, trapping the queen. * 5...Nxe5 is better, but allows White to seize the f7 pawn and trade queens (5...Nxe5 6. Nxe5 dxe5 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 [to keep guarding the queen] 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8). The danger after both 4...Be7? and 4...Ngf6? comes from the threat of dxe5, so one option for Black is to play [[/4...exd4|'''4...exd4''']] first, eliminating the pawn. Then Black is free to develop their minor pieces. The most common line is [[/4...c6|'''4...c6''']]. == 4...Be7? ==
This move, developing the king's bishop to its only available square, may look natural but is a mistake. 

It immediately loses at least a pawn, because after [[/5. dxe5|''5. dxe5'']] retaking the pawn in either way (...dxe5 or ...Nxe5) fails and White wins a minor piece tactically. Black's position is simply too passive to defend against the tactical threats.

== 5. dxe5 ==
White opens the centre to capitalise on Black's passive development. This move comes with a specific tactical threat: by opening the d-file, White hopes to threaten f7, and so force Black to make material concessions. 

[[/5...dxe5|'''5. dxe5??''']] is therefore a mistake, because it allows White to play 6. Qd5!, forming a battery and threatening Qxf7#.

[[/5...Nxe5|'''5. Nxe5?''']] is little better: after 6. Nxe5 dxe5 White could trade queens, but better is 7. Qh5 (threatening Qxf7+) g6 8. Qxe5 Nf6{{chess/not|only}}, winning two pawns.

The engine line is for Black to give up on recovering the pawn for now and focus on activating their pieces.

== 7.Qh5 ==
This move forks e5 and f7. Since Black cannot allow Qxf7, the only sane move is 7...g6, allowing Qxe5. White is a pawn up, though the game is far from over.

== 5. dxe5 ==

The critical move. White opens the centre and attacks Black's knight on f6. 

The pawn must be retaken.:
* Simply moving the knight loses more material to exd6 and/or Bxf7+, e.g. '''5...Ng4?''' 6. Bxf7+ Kxf7 7. Ng5+ Ke8 8. Ne6 (forking Q and B){{Chess/not|+++}}. 
* Black may think White's e-pawn is hanging and that 5...Nxe4?? kills two birds with one stone. However, 6. Qd5! threatens Qxf7# while forking the knight on e4. 6...Qe7 7. Qxe4{{Chess/not|+++}}. 

These leaves Black with two ways to take the pawn on e5.

* [[/5...dxe5|'''5...dxe5??''']] is a mistake because White can launch a winning attack f7. 6. Ng5! and White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 and Black's queen is trapped. 
** 6...Nb6 is the best attempt. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8{{Chess/not|+++}} White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 
** 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4. 
* [[/5...Nxe5|'''5...Nxe5''']] is Black's best move. It recaptures the pawn and attacks White's bishop, so White isn't in time to play 6. Ng5. However, after 6. Nxe5 dxe5 White is able to win at least a pawn tactically.

== 5...Nxe5 ==
By recapturing the pawn with the knight, Black prevents 6. Ng5: this is because Black's knight is gaining time on White's bishop. 

'''6...Bb3?''' concedes the initiative and gives Black time to develop. After 7. Bg4{{Chess/not|=}} pinning the knight, White still cannot play Ng5. 

Therefore White must trade knights, [[/6. Nxe5|'''6. Nxe5''']] dxe5. This is to White's advantage as they will be able to leverage the open d-file to win a pawn (7. Bxf7+).

== 6...dxe5 ==
Black recaptures on e5. 

There are two tactical features that stand out for White in this position: the queens see each other, and White's bishop is threatening Bxf7+. It might seem that these moves could be played in either order to win a pawn, however '''7. Qxd8+?''' Kxd8 8. Bxf7 allows Black to play 8...Nxe4 and recover the material. 

The better order is [[/7. Bxf7|'''7. Bxf7+''']] Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 and White is in time to play 9. Nc3 or 9. f3 to defend e4. 

Despite appearances, 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 is not a mistake due to deflection, as after 8. Qxd8 Black has 8...Bb4+ discovering an attack on d8 and guaranteeing they recover the queen.

== 7. Bxf7+ ==
White takes a pawn with check. This leads to a queen trade. 

If [[/7...Ke7|'''7...Ke7''']], to avoid the check while keeping contact with the queen, 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8. The queens have been traded and White is up a pawn. 

If [[/7...Kxf7|'''7...Kxf7''']] 8. Qxd8, for a moment White may think they have driven away the defender of Black's queen, but Black has 8...Bb4+ (discovered attack on White's queen) 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn.

== 7...Kxf7 ==
Black takes the bishop. This moves the king away from defence of the queen: Black can tactically win it back, but only by giving back the bishop too, and White will be up a pawn. 

[[/8. Qxd8|'''8. Qxd8''']] discharges the tension between the queens. Black can take back via 8...Bb4+, discovering an attack on White's queen. White can defend the check and remove the queen at the same time: 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn. 

If White avoids the queen trade, they are down a bishop for only a pawn.

== 8...Bb4+ ==
Black discovers an attack on White's queen with check. 

If White blocks the check with '''9. Nc3??''', '''9. Nd2??''', or by moving their king, they lose their queen back to ...Rxd8 and are down a bishop. 

If '''9. c3?''' to block the check while counter-attacking the bishop, then after ...Rxd8 cxb4 Nxe4! White has recovered the bishop but Black regains the pawn. The material and position is equal. 

The best move is [[/9. Qd2|'''9. Qd2''']]: interposing the check, counter-attacking Black's bishop ''while also'' avoiding ...Rxd8. After 9...Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 (defends the e-pawn), the queens and bishops are effectively traded and White remains up a pawn. good.

== 5...dxe5?? ==
This seems to recover the pawn but loses tactically because the pressure White exerts on f7. 

[[/6. Ng5|'''6. Ng5!''']] launches a winning attack. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 trapping Black's queen. 
* 6...Nb6 is the best attempt at defence. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8{{Chess/not|+++}} White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 
* 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

== 6. Ng5 ==
Black cannot guard f7. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 and Black's queen is trapped. 

'''6...Nb6''' is the best attempt. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8{{Chess/not|+++}} White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 

'''6...Bb4+''' at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nd7|Hanham variation]] → [[../|4. Bc4]] }} == 4...exd4 == Black trades away White's d4 pawn. This allows Black to develop their knight and bishop without facing dxe5, which would open up a range of tactical possibilities for White. White has two ways to recapture the pawn, with the knight, [[/5. Nxd4|'''5. Nxd4''']], or the queen, [[/5. Qxd4|'''5. Qxd4''']]. Both are viable: if White intends to long castle, 5. Qxd4 might be preferred. After recapturing, White is ready to castle and bring out their remaining minor pieces, and Black must catch up in development. Black intends ...Ngf6, ...Be7, then ...Nb6 to open up a line to develop the queen's bishop. While White's bishop is on c4, ...Nb6 comes with tempo. After either 5. Nxd4 or 5. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Morphy Gambit |parent=[[../|Philidor Defence: Exchange Variation]] }} == 4.Bc4!? · Morphy Gambit == White declines to immediately recapture on d4, instead playing Bc4 and offering the pawn for rapid development and pressure on f7. This gambit, famously used by Paul Morphy to defeat the strong English player Thomas Wilson Barnes, exemplifies classical principles of rapid piece activity and initiative over material. By inviting 4...Nf6 and responding with Ng5, White can generate swift threats before Black finishes development. If Black tries to hold the pawn with 4...c5 or 4...Nc6, they risk falling into a cramped and vulnerable position. The safest course for Black is often to return the pawn and prioritize development with 4...Be7 and short castling. While not a mainline weapon at the highest level, the Morphy Gambit is a sharp and historically rich choice that can punish slow or passive responses. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Exchange variation |parent=[[../|Exchange variation]] }} == 4. Nxd4 == White recaptures the pawn with the knight. [[4...Nf6|'''4...Nf6''']] is the main move, attacking the e4 pawn, and is answered with 5. Nc3 to defend it. To bring more pressure to it, Black must bring the rook to e8, which requires the manoeuvre ...Be7, ...O-O, ...Re8 and ...Bf8. Both sides develop their pieces: Black usually avoids playing ...Nc6 until after they have played ...c5 (with tempo on White's knight) to avoid blocking it in. ...c5 weakens the d6 pawn so committing to it too early can be a mistake, e.g. 4...Nf6 5. Nc3 c5? 6. Bb5+ Bd7 (prevents Q from seeing d6) 7. Nf5 Nc6 8. Nxd6+ Bxd6 9. Qxd6{{Chess/not|++}}. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4'''

Black deliberately weakened his king-side to keep chances at the center. :[[/4. dxe5/]] isn't the best solution. After 4...fxe4, the knight is forced to move to d4 or d2, blocking queen's attack against the Black pawn. Then, Black can rebuild his center with d5. A few games have been tried with 5. Ng5 where Black development is made harder by the White pawn. :[[/4. exf5/]] may lead to weird pawn structures in both camps. If 4...exd4 5. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Mayet attack |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C40]] |parent=[[../|Latvian gambit]] }} == 3. Bc4 · Mayet attack == White declines Black's gambit and instead develops a bishop, preparing Nxe5 with a threat on f7. [[/3...fxe4|'''3...fxe4''']] is Black's best and main move, otherwise why would Black have bothered with attacking White's e4 pawn? However Black has a few alternatives to consider: * '''3...Nf6?''', the '''Morgado Defence''', is the most common amateur move. It is usually played by people who are used to the Latvian gambit accepted. * '''3...Nc6''' transposes into the '''Rousseau gambit''' of the Italian game. * '''3...b5!?''' is the rare and dubious '''Strautins gambit''', which triest to distract the White bishop from the a2-f7 diagonal. === History === Berliner chess master Carl Mayet reached this position in 1837 (via the move order 2. Bc4 and 3. Nf3).[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1336585 Mayet v Hanstein, 1837. Chessgames.com] Gioachino Greco described a game in this line from 1620.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1481289 NN vs Greco, Chessgames.com] == Sample game == {{Chess/board|moves=1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 |float=right |caption=Position after 4...Qg5 |frame=1}} '''NN vs Gioachino Greco
Rome, 1620''' '''1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 f5 3. Bc4''' Today known as the Mayet attack, White declines the gambit and develops a piece instead. '''3...fxe4 4. Nxe5''' White threatens 5. Nf6, forking Black's queen and knight. '''4...Qg5?!''' Black attacks the knight on e5 and the g2 pawn. This sets a trap in that 5. Nf7? is still available, still forking the queen and rook. 5...Qxg2 and: * White may calculate that they are up material after 6. Nxh8?? Qxh1+ 7. Ke2 Qxh2 8. Bxg8??, but their king is too vulnerable and Black has a devastating attack. 8...d5 and if White tries to extract their knight, 9. Nf6 Bg4+ leads to mate. * 6. Rf1 to save the knight and 6...d5 7. Bxd5? Bg4! (attacks queen) 8. f3{{chess/not|only}} Be7 and 9. fxg4?? or 9. Nxh8?? are mate in two (9...Bh4+ 10. Rf2 Qxf2#), 4...d5, the Polerio-Svedenborg variation, is considered more accurate. '''5. d4 Qxg2!?''' This is the sharp poisoned pawn variation. '''6. Qh5+''' An important intermezzo. 6. Rf1 affords Black time to play 6...Nf6 and defend their kingside. '''6...g6{{chess/not|only}} 7. Bf7+ Kd8''' Safer than 7...Ke7, where 8. Qh4+! can't be met with 8...Be7. '''8. Bxg6 Qxh1+ 9. Ke2 Qxc1 10. Nf7+ Ke8 11. Qe5+?''' An error. Better was 11. Nxh8+ discovered check immediately. 11...hxg6 12. Qxg6+ Kd8 13. Nf7+ Ke7 14. Nc3 threatening Nd5+ {{Chess/not|+}}. {{clear}} {{Chess/board |moves=1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.d4 Qxg2 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Bf7+ Kd8 8.Bxg6 Qxh1+ 9.Ke2 Qxc1 10.Nf7+ Ke8 11.Qe5+ Ne7 |caption=Position after 11. Ne7. |float=right |frame=1}} '''11...Ne7!''' Rather than block the check with 11...Be7?. '''12. Nxh8+ hxg6''' White's attack has disappeared. '''13. Nc3 Qxc2+ 14. Ke1 Qxb2 15. Nxe4''' Threatening Nf6+ Kd8 Nf7#. '''15...Qxa1+ 16. Ke2 Qxa2+ 0-1''' White resigns. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} {{ChessMid}} == References == {{reflist}} === See also === == External links == *[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?node=1622261 Games in Mayet attack], Chessgames.com {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

== 4. Nxe5 ==
Now White takes Black's pawn and threatens Nf7, which would fork Black's queen on d8 and rook on h8. Black can choose to defend this threat, ignore the threat or set a trap.

'''[[/4...d5|4...d5]]''', the '''Polerio-Svedenborg variation''', directly defends against the Nf7 threat by blocking the bishop on c4's vision of f7 and attacking it. This is the most common move by far.

'''[[/4...Qg5|4...Qg5!?]]''' sets a trap. It seems to blunder the fork 5. Nf7?!, but after 5...Qxg2! 6. Rf1 Bg4! Black has an attack where White has to be precise. 

'''[[/4...Nf6|4...Nf6?]]''', the '''Corkscrew countergambit''', is just too much. After 5. Nf7 Qe7 6. Nxh8, Black plays the Corkscrew Gambit with 6...d5 and hopes for 7. Bb3?? Bg4!, but if 7. Be2! is played the gambit is proven unsound and Black is down a rook.

= Latvian Gambit, Leonhardt Variation =
==6. Ne3==
White has seemingly thwarted ...d5 yet again, and is now asking the Black army how they're going to save Private Ryan on e4.

There are two options for Black: abandon e4 and make another non-developing move with [[/6...c6/]] to finally establish an iron grip over d5, or continue the charge with [[/6...d5/]], the Atars Gambit, accepting the loss of the d-pawn and saddling White with only the minor inconvenience of having to come and capture it.

It should be pointed out here that, in fact, the suicidal-looking 6...d5 is one of Black's last remaining attempts to revive the Latvian Gambit. If it doesn't work, the swashbuckling old opening will likely be tucked away on a shelf with a label "suitable only for unprepared opponents".

== 2... h6?! · Truck Defense ==
The '''Truck Defense''' involves giving up the central pawn on '''e5''', allowing the white knight to occupy the square. This defense is very rarely played and considered an offbeat opening. It is not commonly seen in high-level tournaments, but can be used to surprise your opponent, especially in casual play.

=== Advantages: ===
One of the key advantages of this defense is that after '''castling on the kingside''', the '''king''' gains an escape square. Additionally, it can help prevent back-rank mates, improving your position as the game progresses. '''The h6 pawn''' controls g5, which allows for moves like '''Nf6''' in response to White's '''Bc4''', preventing the bishop's attack on the f7 square after '''Ng5'''.

=== Disadvantages: ===
The biggest disadvantage of the '''Truck Defense''' is that you end up '''down by one pawn''' material-wise. Also, you will lack central pieces early on, while White will gain an advantage in terms of both '''pawns and knights'''. This can lead to a difficult middle game where White has a better position; '''g6 square''' becomes weak, allowing White to potentially exploit this vulnerability for an attack.

==== Example Continuations: ====


1. e4 e5

2. Nf3 h6

3. Nxe5 Qe7

4. d4 d6

5. Nf3 Qxe4+  

Here, Black can reclaim the pawn they lost, but according to Stockfish, White is still 100 to 200 centipawns ahead, meaning White retains a strong position.

Black can also continue with '''3... d6'''. But...

'''3... f6??'''

A critical mistake! White can deliver a '''checkmate in 6 moves''':

1. Qh5+ g6

2. Qxg6+ Ke7

3. Qf7+ Kd6

4. Nc4+ Kc5

5. Qd5+ Kb4

6. Qa5#

= The Basman Attack =
'''The Basman Attack''' is an unusual chess opening named after the English International Master [[wikipedia:Michael_Basman|Michael John Basman]] who played the strange 2. Nh3 in a game versus John T Fletcher in 2013. 

The Basman Attack is offbeat, but slightly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the [[wikipedia:Ruy_Lopez|Ruy Lopez]] or the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5|Sicilian Defense]]: Najdorf Variation. White intends to play f2-f4 soon.

The Basman Attack incurs multiple problems for White. First, it develops a piece towards the outer edge of the board. The problem with developing your knight to h3 instead of f3 is that on h3 it doesn't control the pivotal central squares of e5 and d4. On h3, the only square the knight can move to that it couldn't move to if it was on f3 is f4. The other problem with this opening is that it loses initiative. In e4 e5 openings, White typically controls the opening. Moves like Nf3 put immediate pressure on the opponent, forcing them to defend. The move Nh3 puts none of that pressure and therefore is an almost pointless move.

It is relatively easy for Black to equalise in this opening, for example, 2...Nf6, 2...d5, and 2...Nc6 all equalise, although Black should be careful to avoid an eventual f2-f4.

=Napoleon Opening or Queen's Attack=
==2. Qf3?!==
The Napoleon Attack, or Napoleon Opening, is weaker than it sounds. Not only does it develop the queen too early, but it blocks the King's Knight from developing to f3, its best square.

As with the similar [[../2. Qh5|2. Qh5]], White hopes for the scholar's mate: 2. Qf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5?? 4.Qxf7#.  In both cases, Black can easily avoid the trap. However, the [[Chess/Parham Attack|Parham Attack]] is more forcing and stronger—first requiring Black to defend his e-pawn (usually with 2...Nc6), then after 3. Bc4 forcing Black to play a sub-optimal move (3...g6 virtually committing Black to a fianchetto rather than a more aggressive placement of the bishop; 3...Qe7 blocking the bishop; or 3...Qf6 taking away the knight's best square). 2. Qf3 places no such impediments on Black's development.

Among serious chess players this opening is very rare, but beginners occasionally play it to troll or surprise the opponent. Black has no problems equalizing this game.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Position |Parham attack |aka=Wayward queen, Danvers, patzer's opening/attack |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] }} == 2. Qh5!? · Parham attack == This is an aggressive opening move that violates an opening principle by bringing the queen out early. So long as Black doesn't fall into White's traps, they will be able to develop easily and play useful moves that gain time on White's queen. 2. Qh5 both attacks the pawn on e5 and puts pressure on f7. The f7 square is the weakest point in Black's position at the start of the game, because it is the only square guarded only by Black's king. White's usual plan is to follow with Bc4 and deal a swift, knock-out blow with Qxf7#, e.g. 2...Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6?? 4. Qxf7#. This is called '''Scholar's mate''' or the '''four-move checkmate'''. === Defend e5 === As f7 is attacked once (by White's queen) and defended once (by Black's king), there is no immediate threat of Qxf7+. However, there is a threat of Qxe5+. [[/2...Nc6|'''2...Nc6''']] is the best move. Black defends against Qxe5+, while also getting to develop a piece to its most active square. The game usually continues 3. Bc4 (bringing a second attacker to f7, so now White really is threatening Qxf7#) g6 (cuts off White's queen's vision of f7, and gains time by forcing the queen to move again) 4. Qf3 (threatens Qxf7# again) Nf6 (blocks White's queen's vision of f7). The immediate threats parried, Black is ready to play ...Bg7 and ...O-O. Other options to defend e5 are playable but come with trade-offs. * '''2...d6''' defends e5, but neglects the opportunity to develop a piece. It also means that if Black wants to play ...d5 later, they will have lost a tempo by taking two moves to play d5 instead of one (d7 to d6 to d5 versus d7 to d5). * '''2...Qf6''' defends both e5 and f7, but violating opening principles yourself is no way to punish your opponent's violations of the same. The queen misplaced on f6 prevents Black's knight from coming there, which it should like to do. If the idea is to trade off queens to end the attack (3. Bc4 g6 4. Qf3 Qxf3 5. Nxf3{{chess/not|+}}), Black is giving White's attack too much credit. * '''2...Qe7''', looks unnatural but is probably fine. === Gambit e5 === Black may try [[/2...Nf6|'''2...Nf6''']], called the '''Kiddie countergambit'''. Black attacks the queen, forcing it to move, but leaves their e-pawn undefended. This is a pawn sacrifice: Black allows White to take the free pawn and instead focuses on developing their pieces. Every time Black gets to play a developing move and White has to move their queen again, Black scores a little victory in the form of tempo. After 3. Qxe5+ Be7 4. Nf3 (say) Nc6 (forces queen to move again) 5. Qf4 O-O{{chess/not}} Black has castled and developed three of their minor pieces as compensation for the lost pawn, and White has largely spent the time moving the same piece around. === Bad moves === [[/2...g6|'''2...g6??''']] is a rookie error. Black attacks the queen and leaves their e-pawn undefended, but moving the g-pawn exposed Black's rook on h8: 3. Qxe5+ Be7 (or 3...Qe7) 4. Qxh8{{Chess/not|+++}}. [[/2...Ke7|'''2...Ke7??''']] is the worst move in the position, 3. Qxe5# is checkmate. === History === 2. Qh5!? is a staple of amateur chess, played against beginners who may be expected to blunder under early pressure. It has a huge number of names, including '''patzer's opening''' (''patzer'', from German ''patzen''[https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/patzer patzer, Collins Dictionary], being a poor chess player), which might mean it is only played ''against'' novices or ''by'' novices. In fact it has seen use by grandmasters as a non-theoretical opening, played not with the expectation that Black will blunder mate in the opening but the understanding that, once Black has parried the first few threats, White still gets a playable position that is about equal. Among its highest-level outings was Magnus Carlsen at the 2018 World Rapid Championship.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1938193 Carlsen v. Vokhidov, 2018] '''Parham''' comes from Bernard Parham (1946―2024), who was a National Master from Indiana who had many original ideas about how chess should be played and the relative values of different pieces. He advocated early queen moves in several lines, including 1. e4 e5 2. Qh5.{{Cite web |title=Bernard Parham, chess innovator, passes away |url=https://thechessdrum.net/blog/2024/06/25/bernard-parham-chess-innovator-passes-away/ |last=Shabazz |first=Daaim |date=2024-06-25 |website=The Chess Drum}} The origin of '''Danvers''', per Winter, has been traced to a 1908 anecdote about a sanatorium:{{Cite web |title=The Danvers Opening (1 e4 e5 2 Qh5) |url=https://chesshistory.com/winter/extra/danvers.html |last=Winter |first=Edward |date=2025-03-20 |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=Chess Notes}}
"Dr E.E. Southard, who was the Harvard College champion for a number of years and who is now a specialist on mental diseases at the Danvers Insane Hospital, tried to explain how his acquaintance with chessplayers assisted him in his profession and why he named his pet début the Danvers Opening, which consists of P-K4 and Q-R5 as White’s first and second moves."

=Parham Attack=
===3... Nf6??===
Black's hotheaded desire to prove that the queen was misplaced and to take the queen has backfired. The next move will be 4.Qxf7# (standing for mate). The one natural developing move leads to mate - and that is why black has to always be careful for '''[[w:Scholar's_mate|Scholar's mate]]'''. 

==Theory table==
'''1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6'''

White only requires one move here: 4. [[/4. Qxf7|Qxf7#]]

==Parham Attack/Scholar's Mate==
===4. Qxf7#===
With this move White gives a checkmate. The Black King cannot take the White queen because the White Bishop on c4 defends it. Further, moving the Black King to e7(Ke7) does not allow it to escape capture on the next move, so this position is checkmate, and White has won the game.

== Parham Attack ==
=== 5. Nc3 ===
Moving the knight to c3 seems natural, since it develops the knight and prevents Black's d-pawn advance. However, this move can be considered a mistake. This is because Black can gain a [[w:Tempo_(chess)|tempo]] by playing [[Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Qh5/2...Nc6/3._Bc4/3...g6/4._Qf3/4...Nf6/5._Nc3/5...Nd4|Nd4!]], moving to an outpost which threatens to win the queen while also threatening to fork white’s pieces at the same time.

== Parham Attack ==
=== 5...Nd4! ===
Black threatens to fork White’s pieces while simultaneously putting pressure on the queen, thereby forcing it to retreat to its original square, resulting in a tempo gain. White has some options, white can respond with [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...Nd4/6. Qd1|Qd1]], which retreats the queen to it’s starting square while keeping pressure over the diagonals and protecting the c2 pawn, or Qd3, which does not retreat the queen and still protects the c2 pawn. However, playing Qd3 results in a loss of control over the diagonals. Everything else loses the rook to 6...Nxc2! and 7...Nxa1.

White has a variety of moves to play here.

* [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...Nd4/6. Qd1|Qd1]]: Qd1 retreats the queen back to the square, saving white from being forked. This move is the best move to play in this position. 

* [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...Nd4/6. Qd3|Qd3]]: An alternative to Qd1, but this lessens the control over the center.

Qf3]] }} == 4...f5 == ...f5 parries the threat of Qf7# by obstructing the queen's vision of the f7 square. It also attacks White's e-pawn, and if Black is able to remove it, they might be able to play d5 and take over the centre. '''5. exf5?!''', thinking to clear the obstruction, is inaccurate, ultimately because it gives up control of the d5 square. Black can't play ...d5 straight away. If 5...d5?!, apparently with tempo on the bishop, then 6. fxg6! and Black doesn't have time to take the bishop because White's ''pawn'' now controls f7: 6...dxc4?? 7. Qf7#!. Instead Black should prepare ...d5 with 5...Nd4 first. This is a double attack on White's queen and the c3 square (threatening ...Nxc3+, Black wins the rook by a fork). Then: * 6. Qd1 to defend the c3 square is most natural, which allows 6...d5. * 6. Qg3!? allows the fork but sets a trap. 6...Nc3+ 7. Kd1 Nxa1?? 8. Qxe5!+ Qe7 9. Qxh8{{Chess/not|+++}}. * 6. Qd5?? threatens 7. Qf7# and Qxe5+. This is very common but strictly inferior, and 7...Qf6 deals with both threats. '''5. Ne2''' is White's best move: controlling d4 so preventing ...Nd4. Then the game may continue 5...Nf6 (threatening ...fxe4, as the knight will prevent vision of f7) 6. Nbc3 (defending e4) d6 7. exf5 Bxf5 8. d3{{Chess/not}} for an even game. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4 g6 4. Qf3 f5'''

==Kiddie Countergambit==
===3. Qxe5+===
White captures the undefended e5 pawn and gives check. There are two ways for Black to respond: 3...Be7 or 3...Qe7?!. 3...Be7 is better, since after 4...Nc6, White will need to spend a tempo retreating the queen. 3...Qe7 allows a queen trade, meaning White no longer needs to spend the tempo retreating, thus giving back the advantage to White. After 3...Qe7 4. Qxe7 Bxe7, White is up a central pawn while Black is barely ahead in development.

=Wayward Queen Attack=
This move is a blunder as it allows 3. Qxe5+! creating a deadly fork to the king and the rook and thus loses that h8 rook. If, however, White blunders and Black plays well, the Queen may be trapped near h8, but this is unlikely.

Instead of playing 2…g6??, 2…Nc6 defends the e-pawn and gives Black a very slight edge due to White’s misplaced queen.

2…Nf6 attacking the Queen thus preventing the famous Scholar's Mate is another idea, though less common. Although this gives White the opportunity to capture on e5, Black in return gains tempos as White’s queen is far from her home and doesn’t have a clear way to get to safe squares such as e2 and d1 safely.

Black also has the ability to play Qe7 attempting to defend the pawn, but it somewhat blunders a whole queen as white can open the bishop to attack the queen on e7 (3. d3/d4, g6 4. Bg5, ...) The queen still has the ability to take, but if the white queen can protect the bishop, the queen will have to go somewhere else, thus it displaces the queen and black is vulnerable to other attacks, if white plays well that is. 

If black plays Nc6, then white can play Bc4. The bishop would be vulnerable to attacks, but if black attempts to do any other move than guard the f-pawn, black loses. (3. Bc4, g6 4. Qf3, d6 (or any other move that doesn't protect the f-pawn) ?? 5. Qf7#, 1-0). If g6 is played, white can retreat to f3, and deliver a checkmate that way.

= Mengarini's Opening =
=== 2. a3 ===
White plays a waiting move instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but timid and concedes White's first move advantage. This is similar to an Open Game with colors reversed, except that White has played a3 to stop Bb4 if Nc3 is played. Black can choose a variety of responses:

* 2...Nf6
* 2...Nc6
* 2...Bc5
* 2...d5
* 2...f5!?

= 2. b3?! Charles' Opening =
'''Charles' Opening''' is an unusual chess opening named after the British chess player and writer [[wikipedia:Charles Williams (British writer)|Charles Williams]] (1886–1945). Although this opening is rarely used, Vilmos Nogrady (as White) played it with mediocre success, tying with Meszaros Gyula in 1993.

== Description ==
Charles' Opening is offbeat, but perfectly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the Ruy Lopez or the Scotch Game: Schmidt Variation, or to surprise the opponent. White intends to play Bb2 soon. After 2...c7-c5, the position is similar to an Anti-Sicilian.

Charles' Opening incurs a couple of problems for White. First, it delays the development of a minor piece, disallowing an early castle for White to bring their king to safety. The other problem is that it removes the advantage White has going first. 2. b3 delays the development of another piece with something like 2. Nf3 or 2. Bc4, instead planning to develop their dark-squared bishop to b2, which gives black more time to develop.

It is relatively easy for Black to equalise in this opening, for example, 2...Nf6, 2...Nc6, and 2...Bc5 all equalise, although Black should be careful to avoid a quick Bb2 and Nf3, putting intense pressure on the pawn on e5.

== Main variations ==
After 1. e4 e5 2. b3, the most important continuations are:

* 2...Nf6 (Main line)
** 3. Bb2 (Classical Variation)
** 3. Nf3 (Wells Variation)
* 2...Nc6 (Fine Defense)
* 2...Bc5 (Bishop's Defense)
*2...f5?! (Cincinnati Gambit)

=== Main line: 2...Nf6 ===
In the main line after 2...Nf6, White has two major options. Either 3. Bb2 or 3. Nf3 offers White good chances for an equal game.

==== Classical Variation: 3. Bb2 ====
The classical variation of the Charles' Opening is the most analyzed variation. After 3. Bb2 Black has 3...Nxe4, 3...Bc5, or 3...Nc6. After 3...Nxe4 play usually continues 4. Qe2 d5 5. Nc3 Bf5 (Black does not play 5...Nxc3 because they wants to hang on to their pawn advantage. Black would lose his pawn advantage after something like 6. Qxe5+ Qe7 7. Qxe7+ Bxe7 8. Bxc3) 6. Nxe4 dxe4 7. Qb5+ Nd7 (once again the best move hanging on to the e5 pawn) 8. Ne2 (White develops his knight instead of playing 8. Qxb7 because Black can play 8...Rb8 9. Qxa7 Bc5 10. Qa4 O-O, where White is up a pawn but Black has a major development lead and White's queen is on the awkward a4 square. The computer sees this position -1. 90 for White.) 8...Rb8 9. h4?! (This move threatens to trap black's dark-squared bishop.) 9...h5 10. O-O-O. The ''Stockfish Engine'' says Black is slightly winning but that is only because of a complicated line after 10...c6. 3...Bc5 is probably the strongest move, since it quickly develops another piece and prepares to play O-O extremely early. After 3...Bc5 play usually continues 4. Nc3 O-O 5. Qe2 Re8 6. O-O-O a5 (a7-a5 is a very good move. It plans to weaken the queenside and break White's fianchetto with an eventual a5-a4) 7. Nf3 d6 (supporting his other central pawn and his developed bishop, while allowing his other, undeveloped bishop to develop) 8. d4 exd4 9. Nxd4 a4 10. Kb1 Nc6 11. Nxc6 bxc6 12. f3 axb3 13. cxb3 Ba3 (trading off one of his most active pieces in order to expose White's king even more) 14. Bxa3 Rxa3 15. Qb2 Rb7 (planning to eventually double up his rooks on the a file with Rea8). The final response to 3. Bb2 is 3...Nc6. After 3...Nc6 play usually continues 4. Nf3 Bc5 5. Bd3 O-O 6. O-O Re8 7. Nc3 d6 8. Na4 (planning to trade their knight for Black's active bishop while activating his bishop on b2) 8...Bg4 9. Nxc5 dxc5 10. a4 Nd4 11. Bxd4 cxd4 12. h3 Bh5. This position is very even. White plans to expand queenside with moves like b3-b4 and a4-a5; Black plans to clamp the center with move like c3-c5 and slowly maneuver his pieces to the kingside for an attack. Overall, the classical variation of the Charles' Opening is the most challenging variation against 2...Nf6. If a player likes lots of opening theory and wants a new weapon for their opening repertoire, the Charles' Opening: Classical Variation is for them. 

==== Wells Variation: 3. Nf3 ====
The Wells variation of the Charles' Opening is playable, but definitely not the best variation after 2...Nf6. The ''Stockfish Engine'' evaluates the position after 3. Nf3 -0. 86 for White. After 3. Nf3 Black has 3...Nxe4, 3...Bc5, or 3...d5. After 3...Nxe4 play usually continues

=== Fine Defense: 2...Nc6 ===
The Fine Defense often transposes to the Classical Variation of the Charles' Opening. For example, after 3. Bb2 Nf6 it is a line in the Classical Variation of the Charles' Opening. However, after 2...Nc6 White can opt not to transpose to the classical variation with 3. Nf3. 3. Nf3 can transpose to the Bishop's defense after 3...Bc5, but the best response for Black is to play 3...Nf6. After 3...Nf6 play usually continues 4. Bb5 Nxe5 5. O-O Nf6 (Black breaks the principle of not moving pieces multiple times in the opening to remove the threat of Re1, hitting the knight and, in the future, putting another attacker on the pawn on e5.) 6. Bxc6 dxc6 7. Nxe5 Bd6 (developing while attacking the knight) 8. Re1 (setting up a discovered check if they move their knight) 8...O-O (moving out of the discovered check) 9. Bb2. The Fine Defense is one of the weaker responses to the Charles' Opening; if you want an opening that is solid, yet can transpose to multiple other variations of the Charles' Opening, then the Fine Defense is for you.

=== Bishop's Defense: 2...Bc5 ===
The Bishop's defense was once used by Jan Sosna in 2018, where they beat Marvin Engert in a game. After 2....Bc5 White has two major options, 3. Nf3 and 3. c3. After 3. Nf3 play usually continues 3...Nc6 4. Bb5 Nge7 5. O-O Nd4 6. Ba3 (Ba3 looks like a strange move, but it has purpose. White plays this move looking to trade off Black's most active piece, their bishop on c4.) 6...Nxf3+ 7. Qxf3 Bxa3 8. Nxa3 O-O. It's hard to decide who's winning this position. White has a lead to development, but their pieces are awkward, with a bishop on b5, pinning nothing, and a knight on a3 that's only useful squares it can see is c4 and b5. 3. c3 is a move that intends to get a big center with an eventual d2-d4. After 3. c3 play will usually continue 3...d5 4. d4 exd4 5. cxd4 Bb4+ 6. Bd2 Bxd2+ 7. Nxd2 dxe4 8. Nxe4 Nf6 9. Nxf6+ Qxf6 10. Nf3 O-O 11. Bc4 Re8+ 12. Ne5 (where White's king is severely exposed and they will have to give up a pawn in order to castle after something like 12...Nd7 13. O-O Nxe5 14. dxe5 Rxe5). Overall, the Bishop's Defense, is one of the more challenging ways to beat the Charles' Opening and is a good tool to have in your opening repertoire.

=== Cincinnati Gambit: 2...f5?! ===
The sharp 2...f5, the Cincinnati Gambit, although somewhat dubious, was played a few times by 1989 Cuban chess champion IM Pedro Paneque Martin, where they once tied with Luis E. Valdes. It may lead to complicated positions and interesting endgames, e.g. 3. exf5 Nf6 4. Bb2 d5!? 5. Bxe5 Bxf5 6. Nf3 Bd6 7. Bd3 Bxd3 8. cxd3 (where White is a pawn up, but has doubled, isolated queen's pawns.) White has multiple ways to decline the gambit. 3. d4, 3. Bb2, and 3. Nc3 are all strong ways for White to decline the gambit. After 3. d4 play usually continues 3...Nf6 4. exf5 exd4 5. Nf3 (White doesn't play 5. Qxd4 because it leaves their queen exposed, allowing black to play normal developing moves like Nc6 while forcing the queen to move) 5...Bb4+ 6. c3 Bxc3+ 7. Nxc3 dxc3 8. Ba3 (White loses a pawn in this line, but has compensation since it's bishop has a strong diagonal on a3, which doesn't let Black play O-O) After 3. Bb2 Black plays 3...Nf6 (Black doesn't play fxe4 because of the deadly 4. Qh5+!!, followed by either 4...g6 5. Qxe5+ Qe7 6. Qxh8, or 4...Ke7 5. Qxe5+ Kf7 6. Bc4+ d5 7. Bxd5+ where black has to sacrifice their queen with 7...Qxd5 in order to not get checkmated or lose even more material) 4. exf5 Nc6 5. Bb5 a6 6. Bxc6 dxc6 7. Bxe5 Bxf5 (where White is a pawn up, but Black has a minor lead in development.) 3. Nc3 is the weakest way to decline the gambit. Play usually will follow with 3...Nf6 4. f4 exf4 5. e5 Ne4 6. Nxe4 fxe4 7. Qe2 d5 8. exd6 Qf6 9. Qxe4 Kd8 (Black doesn't play 9...Be6 because 10. dxc7 Nc6 11. Ba6!! where White has a major advantage of roughly +3. 75) 10. dxc7+ Kxc7 11. d4 Bd6 (In this position, Black is a pawn down and can no longer castle, but will gain a lead in development since White's queen is exposed so moves like Bf5 force it to move.) Overall, the Cincinnati Gambit is rarely played, but is an interesting opening that is laced with tricks and traps.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Centre pawn opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] }} == 2. c3?! · Centre pawn opening == White wishes to build a big, two-pawn centre, and plays 2. c3?! to support pushing the pawn to d4. This idea, c3 to support d4, is a common plan for White in many open games (games beginning [[../|1. e4 e5]]): c3 after developing the knight is the Ponziani ([[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3|2. Nf3 Nc6 3. c3]]), and it comes after developing the knight and bishop in the Italian and Spanish games ([[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3|3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3]] or e.g. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5/4. c3|3. Bb5 Bc5 4. c3]]3...Bc5 is a sideline today, the classical defence. The same idea occurs in the main line later: 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Re1 b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. c3, but the line is longer and makes for a worse illustration of the point.). However, played on White's second move without any pieces developed, it is simply too slow. Black can respond vigorously with '''2...d5''' to eliminate transpositional possibilities. After 3. exd5 Qxd5{{chess/not|-}}, there is no 4. Nc3 to chase the queen away and gain a tempo as the c3 pawn is occupying the square. Staunton suggested that by avoiding taking the pawn, White could keep the game competitive: 3. Nf3 dxe4 4. Nxe5 Bd6!? 5. Nc4 Be6 6. d4 exd3 e.p. 7. Bxd3{{chess/not|+}}. However, 4...Qe7! is an improvement, which forces White to move the knight again and gums up White's play for the centre, as d4 will be met with exd3 e.p. and a discovered check. Black sweeps ahead in development to a reach a dominating position. 5. Nc4 Nc6 6. Be2 Bf5 7. O-O O-O-O{{chess/not|-}}. === History === {{Chess/board |moves=1. e4 e5 2. c3 Nf6 3. Qc2 Bc5 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Bb5 d6 6. d4 exd4 7. cxd4 Bb4+ 8. Nc3 Bd7 9. O-O |caption=Position given by Ruy López. |frame=1 |float=right}} 2. c3?! is very unusual today but has a long history. It is the first opening [[w:Ruy López de Segura|Ruy López de Segura]] chose to cover in his 1561 treatise, where he gives the line 2...Nf6 3. Qc2 Bc5 4. Nf3 Nc6 (López gives 4...Qe7 5. d4?? exd4 with threat of ...Qxe4 as an improvement for Black) 5. Bb5 d6 (a mistake, given it pins the knight) 6. d4 exd4 7. cxd4 Bb4+ 8. Nc3 Bd7 9. O-O{{chess/not|++}}.{{Cite book |title=The Art of the Game of Chess |last=López |first=Ruy |publisher=The Catholic University of America Press |year=2020 |location=Washington D.C. |pages=119-120 |orig-date=1561 |translator-last1=McGrath |translator-first1=Michael J.}} However, López reckoned without the reply 2...d5. By the time of [[w:François-André Danican Philidor|Philidor]] this was known to be the best retort, and on account of ...d5 he dismissed 2. c3?! as "very ill played."{{Cite book |title=Analysis of the game of chess |last=Philidor |first=F. A. D. |publisher=P. Elmsly |year=1790 |location=London |pages=50-63 |url=https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_analysis-of-the-game-of-_philidor-f-d-franco_1790_1}} After this discovery the opening must have fallen out of fashion. When [[w:Howard Staunton|Staunton]] analysed the opening in his 1847 book{{Cite book |title=The Chess-Player's Handbook |last=Staunton |first=Howard |publisher=Henry G. Bohn |year=1847 |location=London |pages=238-243 |url=https://archive.org/details/chessplayershan00staugoog}} (calling it the "'''the queen's bishop's pawn opening'''"), he offered a survey of previous analyses and surmised,
"This mode of commencing the battle was probably a favourite in the early days of European chess play, as Ruy Lopez has devoted more than ordinary space and attention to it in his often-quoted work of the sixteenth century."
Eric Schiller re-christened 2. c3 after '''MacLeod Call''', who "was not a very good player, but he was persistent in his use of this opening. At the 6th American Chess Congress of 1889, he relied on his pet opening, but finished at the bottom of the crosstable."{{Cite book |title=Unorthodox Chess Openings |last=Schiller |first=Eric |publisher=Cardoza Publishing |year=1998 |pages=239}} In recent years some databases have begun to call this, confusingly, the "'''Lopez opening'''". Unlikely to be in reference to Ruy López's book (from which 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 is the better known line, which more usually bears his name), the misunderstanding may have arisen from [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talk:Centre_Pawn_Opening&oldid=1101331183#Requested_move_22_July_2022 a longstanding editorial gaffe at Wikipedia]. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. c3'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|The Whale |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=
* [[../|Open game]] * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. c4|English opening]] }} == 2. c4?! · The Whale == White controls d5 another time with a pawn instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but slow. It concedes White's first move advantage and has the drawbacks of creating a permanent hole on d4 and blocking the f1 bishop from developing to c4 or b5. Black has a wide range of reasonable options, including '''2...Bc5''', '''2...Nf6''', or '''2...Nc6'''. [[/2...g6|'''2...g6?!''']] is called the '''Adorjan defence'''. This prepares to fianchetto, though the king's bishop could already develop along the a3-f8 diagonal, and invites 3. d4! exd4 4. Qxd4 with tempo on the rook on h8. 4...Nf6 5. Bg5 where 5...Bg7?? loses a piece to 6. e5{{chess/not|+++}}. [[/2...c6|'''2...c6?!''']] transposes into the open variation of the accelerated Panov attack, though this improves White's position. Playing [[/2...d5|'''2...d5?''']] anyway is called the '''Bavarian gambit'''. === History === [[w:John Cochrane (chess player)|John Cochrane]] (1798―1878) experimented with this opening.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1271849 John Cochrane v Howard Staunton, 1842. Chessgames.com] The name, "The Whale", was coined by offbeat opening aficionado Eric Schiller, writing, "It seems to me rather large and lumbering... [https://ratings.fide.com/profile/2011204 Jennie Frenklakh] who lives close to whale territory in California played it in her early years".{{Cite book |title=Unorthodox Chess Openings |last=Schiller |first=Eric |publisher=Cardoza Publishing |year=1998 |isbn=0-940685-73-6 |location=New York |pages=143-144}} == References == {{Reflist}} === See also === {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Leonardis variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] }} == 2. d3 · Leonardis variation == This insipid move is playable but concedes White's first move advantage. Inferior to most other responses to 1. e4 e5, 2. d3 defends e4, though it was not under attack. While it opens a line for the queen's side bishop to develop, it closes the line 1. e4 opened for the king's bishop. Should White wish to play d4 in the future, they have lost a tempo here. White misses the opportunity to develop a piece to make an unnecessary pawn move instead. Black is allowed easy equality with '''2...Nc6''' or '''2...Nf6''' followed by 3...d5. This can lead to a position like a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6|Philidor defence]] with colours reversed: e.g. 2...Nf6 3. Nf3 Nc6 4. Be2 d5 5. Nbd2{{chess/not|-}} is the reversed Hanham variation. If White doesn't want to develop their king's bishop to e2 behind the pawn chain, their intention may to be to play in the manner of a King's Indian attack, where White builds a d3 and e4 pawn chain and the fianchettos the bishop to g2: though the move order [[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...d5/2. g3|1. Nf3 (preventing e5) d5 2. g3]] is more accurate. There are also plans involving an early f4, a sort of inferior [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4|Vienna gambit]], which are still equal but less popular. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. d3'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Centre game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21–C22]] |parent=[[../|Open Game]] }} == 2. d4 · Centre game == White plays '''2. d4''' to smash open the centre. White threatens to take on e5, but really they are provoking exd4, and planning to develop their pieces rapidly by opening up the d-file for their queen and bishop. White may yet gambit some pawns for even faster development. This is the explosive Centre game. Black has some options, but almost always takes the pawn. === Take the pawn === [[/2...exd4|'''2...exd4''']], the Centre game accepted, is Black's most common and objectively best move. This leads to several different sorts of game depending on how White would like to recapture. Recapturing immediately, 2. Qxd4, is most common. Sounder is to play 2. Nf3 first, intending to recapture the pawn with the knight, but the most aggressive continuation is is 2. c3, gambitting one or two pawns in exchange for getting a huge development lead. === Defend e5 === If Black doesn't take on d4, next turn White will be able to take Black's e5 pawn instead. So if Black doesn't want to accept the centre game, they have to find a way to defend e5: 2...d6?!, 2...f6?, or 2...Nc6. [[/2...d6|'''2...d6?!''']] defends with a pawn, but it is not ideal. White can take on e5 anyway, and after the d-pawn recaptures, trade queens and force Black to give up their castling rights: 3. dxe5 dxe5 4. Qxd8+ Kxd8. Alternatively. White can transpose into a Philidor defence with 3. Nf3. 2...d6?! is a transposition into the Maróczy defence, usually seen in the Pirc in the move order [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4|1. e4 d6 2. d4]] e5). '''2...f6?''' is much worse of course, as the f-pawn makes a lousy defender of the e-pawn. After 3. dxe5, Black dare not retake with the f pawn or face Qh5+! with their weakened kingside (see also the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6|Damiano defence]]). The best way to defend is the most flexible, [[/2...Nc6|'''2...Nc6''']]. This transposes into a line in the Nimzowitsch defence called the Kennedy variation (usually seen via 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 e5?!). If 3. dxe5, Black can retake 3...Nxe5, but may then be forced to move the knight again by 4. f4. Alternatively White can choose 3. d5, kicking the knight, which Black then reroutes to g6 via e7. If Black wishes to avoid accepting the Centre game then 2...Nc6 is probably their best alternative with the most practical chances. === Gambit e5 === If Black is having a fun time trading pawns in the centre of the board, or thinks that having a well-contested, even game might be too boring for them, Black may decide to just give up on e5 and counterattack instead. These moves are invariably bad. [[/2...d5|'''2...d5?''']] is the Beyer gambit. The idea is that if White takes the d5 pawn instead of the e5 pawn, Black can bring out their queen: 3. exd5? Qxd5 4. Nc3 (attacking queen) Qxd4 5. Qxd4 exd4{{Chess/not}}. Black gets an even endgame. Of course if White takes the e5 pawn as they had planned, this gambit is just bad. 3. dxe5 dxe4 4. Qxd8+ Kxd8 and White gets a favourable queen trade, forcing Black to lose castling rights. '''2...f5?''', sabotaging Black's own kingside, is simply losing whether White takes the e5 ''or'' the f5 pawn. === History === This opening had fallen out of favour by the early 20th century when it was thought White was unable to prove an advantage. It had some critical re-appraisal in the 1980s but remains a distant fifth sideline behind White's other second moves. == Theory table == '''1. e4 e5 2. d4''' {| class="wikitable" |- !   !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! == 2...d6 ==
This is an inferior way to enter a Philidor. While White's best move is still Nf3, transposing into the Philidor, it gives the additional option of immediately entering an endgame with 3.dxe5 dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 5.Bc4 (though engines have no trouble defending it for Black). Black would lose the right to castle, and White would have a lead in development. White can also enter a Chekhover-like position via 3.Nc3 exd4 4.Qxd4 with the intention to respond to Nc6 with a Bb5 pin, or alternatively drawing the queen back to d3 or e3 and simply enjoying a space advantage. As such, it is considered strictly inferior to the Philidor move order, because White's alternatives after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 are much less aggressive.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Centre game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[../|Centre game]] }} == 2...exd4 == Black takes White's d-pawn. === Retake the pawn === [[/3. Qxd4|'''3. Qxd4''']] is the main move. This allows Black to develop 3...Nc6 with tempo, forcing White to move their queen again. [[/3. Nf3|'''3. Nf3''']], the '''Kieseritzky variation''', allows White to prepare to retake the pawn with the knight instead. This avoids giving Black ...Nc6 with tempo. 3...Bb4+ or 3....Bc4 are playable, or there are several possible transpositions including 3...Nc6, transposing to the Scotch game, 3...d6 to the Philidor defence, and 3...Nf6 to the modern attack in the Russian game. === Gambit the pawn === [[/3. c3|'''3. c3''']] is the '''Danish gambit'''. White offers to let Black keep the pawn in return for rapid development. They may gambit one (3...dxc3 4. Nxc3) or two (3...dxc3 4. Bc4 cxb2 5. Bxc2) pawns in this way. This is playable, and White gets a lot of piece activity in compensation for the pawn(s). [[/3. Bc4|'''3. Bc4''']], the '''von der Lasa gambit''', is also playable. An independent line follows 3...Bb4+, but usually this transposes into one of several different gambits. If 3...Nf6, White can transpose into the Urusov gambit with 4. Nf6 (4. e5?! and Black is better after 4...d5!). After 3...Nc6 instead, White may yet play c3 and transpose into the Göring gambit (4. c3 dxc3 5. Nf3, with the idea 5...cxb2 6. Bxb2), or otherwise transpose into the Scotch (4. Nf3 Nf6, where the choice is 5. e5 or gambit the e-pawn as well with 5. O-O). [[/3. f4|'''3. f4?''']] is the '''Halasz-McDonnell gambit'''. Having deflected Black's pawn away from control of f4, White seizes space on the king's side. This gives Black time to defend their pawn, 3...Nc6, and they can gain initiative attacking e4, 4. Nf3 d5!, because White cannot defend it with Nc3 until they have removed Black's d4-pawn. Against best play White is not thought to have compensation for the pawn. [[/3. Bd3|'''3. Bd3''']] is the '''Ross gambit'''. This is a less ambitious square for the bishop. Black can defend the pawn with 4. Nc6 and White has partial compensation. ==Theory table== '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4''' {| class="wikitable" |- !   !! 3 !! 4 !! Evaluation !! Notes |- ! [[Chess/Center Game|Center Game]] | '''[[/3. == 3. Bf4?! — Boyard Gambit ==
'''3. Bf4?!''' develops the bishop to f4 instead of immediately recapturing the pawn, offering the '''Boyard Gambit'''.


=== (Its a custom opening) ====== Responses: ===
'''3...d5''' strengthens Black's center and supports further development.

'''3...Nc6''' develops a knight and defends the d4 pawn.

'''Downsides:''' White voluntarily delays recovering the d4-pawn, allowing Black to consolidate the extra material and develop with an advantage if White cannot generate enough activity.

An independent line is '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Bf4?! Nc6'''.

The '''Boyard Gambit''' is characterized by '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Bf4?!'''.

(unknown origin - not officially named yet)

An independent line is '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Bf4?! Nc6 4. Nf3 Bb4+ 5. Nbd2 Nf6 6. Bd3 O-O 7. O-O''' where White has rapid development and active pieces but Black has successfully retained the extra pawn.

=== Why it is dubious: ===
The '''Boyard Gambit''' is considered '''dubious''' because White gives Black a clear material advantage without an immediate tactical justification. White hopes that the lead in development and active pieces will provide enough compensation for the pawn, but Black can often consolidate the extra material with accurate play.

The central problem with '''3.Bf4?!''' is that White's compensation is uncertain. In the normal development of the position, White would usually prefer to recover the d4-pawn or use the tempo to create an immediate tactical threat. '''Bf4''' does neither directly.

The '''Boyard Gambit''' is an offbeat and '''dubious''' gambit characterized by '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Bf4?!''', where White sacrifices the immediate recovery of the d4-pawn in exchange for development and attacking chances.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Kieseritzky variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[../|Center game accepted]]}} == 3. Nf3 · Kieseritzky variation == White brings another attacker to Black's d4 pawn. This often transposes to other openings, though independent lines exist. [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']] is the most common move, transposing to the Scotch game, more normally seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4. [[/3...Bc5|'''3...Bc5''']] is another normal move, developing the bishop. This can go two ways; 4. Nxd4 Nc6 transposes into the Classical Scotch game, while 4. c3 is the Lanc-Arnold gambit, an independent option. === History === [[w:Lionel Kieseritzky|Lionel Kieseritzky]] (1806-1853) was a German chess master. Kiesertizky played this line in a blind simul in 1851, and annotated and published the game in ''La Régence'', the chess journal he edited.{{Cite journal |title=Parties entre les plus forts joueurs de l'epoque |journal=La Régence; journal des échecs |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_UBRBAAAAYAAJ |volume= |issue=5 |pages=137-154 |year=1851}} (Game is No. CLXXI pp 149-150)[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2798196 Kieseritzky v Witcomb, 1851. Chessgames.com] == Sample game == '''Lionel Kieseritzky vs Henry Witcomb'''
'''21 April 1851. Blind simul.''' {{Chess/board|moves=1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Nf3 c5 4. Bc4 d6 5. Ng5 Nh6 6. c3 Nc6 7. f4 Na5 8. Bd5 Bg4 9. Qa4+ Bd7 10. Qc2 dxc3 11. Nxc3 f6 12. O-O|caption=In this position, Black plays 12...fxg5? and loses.|frame=1|float=right}} '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Nf3''' White prepares to recapture the pawn with the knight instead of the queen. This gives Black the opportunity to defend and hold on to the pawn. '''3...c5 4. Bc4 d6 5. Ng5 Nh6''' White makes an attack on the f7 square with knight and bishop; Black defends. '''6. c3 Nc6 7. f4''' "A necessary move to prevent the Knight from moving to d5," Kieseritzky explains (translated). '''7...Na5 8. Bd5 Bg4 9. Qa4+ Bd7 10. Qc2 dxc3 11. Nxc3 f6??''' A mistake to give up control of the e6 square. In addition, the pawn is not really threatening to take the knight yet (see game continuation). '''12. O-O''' This sets a trap by allowing Black to take the knight. An alternative is 12. Ne6, attacking the queen. 12...Bxe6 13. Bxe6 and the bishop dominates Black's king and is difficult to dislodge (13...Qe7 14. Nd5! prevents ...Qxe6 due to Nc7+ winning the queen. 13...Nc6 intending ...Nd4 is stymied by 14. Be3.) 12...Qc8 13. f5 secures the outpost for white. '''13...fxg5? 13. fxg5''' Black now must move or lose the defender of the f7 square. Black could have limped on if they had instead given room to their king: 13...Qe7 14. Nf3 {{chess/not|+++}}. '''13...Ng4?? 14. Bf7+ Ke7 15. Nd5#''' "Capital error," writes Kieseritzky of 13...Ng4??. He advises Black should have given up the piece with 13...Qb6 14. gxh6 O-O-O to allow the game to continue and "conditions would be equal for both sides." Kieseritzky underestimates his position: material may be equal but White is completely dominant. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=3...Nc6 4. Nxd4 Nf6 |name1=Scotch game, Schmidt variation
(by transposition) |line2=3...Bc5 4. Nxd4 Nc6 |name2=Scotch game, Classical variation
(by transposition) |line3=3. ... ... 4. c3 |name3=Lanc-Arnold gambit }} {{ChessMid}} == References == {{reflist}} === See also === {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}} {{BookCat}}

By far, the most popular move is '''4. Qe3''' – Paulsen's Attack – lining up the queen with Black's king. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Danish Gambit |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4|Centre game]] → |responses=
* [[/3...dxc3|3...dxc3 · Danish Gambit Accepted]] * [[/3...d5|3...d5 · Sörensen Defence]] * [[/3...Ne7|3...Ne7 · Svenonius Defence]] }} == 3. c3 · Danish gambit == This is an aggressive gambit which, if accepted, leads to a tactical game. Before retaking the pawn, White allows Black to take a second one first. White hopes to use the tempi to get their pieces developed, while Black busy capturing pawns. After [[/3...dxc3|'''3...dxc3''']], '''accepting''' the gambit, White has two choices. After 4. Nxc3, Black is up a pawn, but in exchange White has a piece developed and is the only one with a pawn in the centre. More common is 4. Bc4, giving Black the chance to win another pawn: 4...cxb2 5. Bxb2, White is down two pawns but in compensation has two pieces developed and centre control. While engines find that Black has a slightly edge in the Danish gambit accepted, the lines are nevertheless dangerous to face because of White's piece activity. Therefore it is more common for Black to '''decline''' the gambit at this stage, with [[/3...d5|'''3...d5''']], the '''Sörensen defence'''. In lieu of giving White piece activity, Black allows White to recover the pawn, 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. cxd4, [[/3...Qe7|'''3...Qe7''']] is an uncommon but sound sideline, where Black stays up one pawn without giving White so much of a development lead. This covers the main moves. Black has a few other moves to give back the pawn, but these are atypical: [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']] is the most common way to decline the gambit at the amateur level. 4. Nf3 transposes to the Göring gambit more commonly seen in the Scotch game move order, which may still be declined with ...d5. Otherwise, 4. cxd4 d5 5. e5, White regains the material and has more space. [[/3...d3|'''3...d3!?''']] to decline the gambit is inferior, as it allows 4. Bxd3, where White both recovers the material and develops a piece. [[/3...Ne7|'''3...Ne7''']] is called the '''Svenonius defence'''. === History === The gambit is named for [[w:Martin Severin From|Martin Severin From]] (1828―1895), a Danish chess master who played it extensively including at a major tournament in Paris in 1867.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?tid=79227 Paris (1867). Nf3 - Rhubarb Gambit]] }} =Danish Gambit Accepted= The Danish Gambit Accepted is popular among club players, but not so popular at the highest level. That is because, it is easy for black to fall into one of the many traps on this line, but if black knows what to do, white can get no more than equality out of the opening. White has two main options from this position: :[[/4. Bc4/|'''4. Bc4''']] - Double Danish Gambit :[[/4. Nxc3/|'''4. Nxc3''']] - Single Danish Gambit Although it may have been known earlier, Danish player Severin From essayed the gambit in an 1867 Paris tournament and he is usually given credit for the opening. The Danish gambit was popular with masters of the attack including Alexander Alekhine, Frank Marshall, Joseph Henry Blackburne, and Jacques Mieses, but as Black's defenses improved it lost favor in the 1920s. Today it is rarely played in top-level chess. White will sacrifice one or two pawns for the sake of rapid development and attack. With care, Black can accept one or both pawns safely, or simply decline the gambit altogether. ==Theory table== '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. c3 dxc3'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Danish Gambit Accepted||rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|pd|pd|pd|pd||pd|pd|pd|||||||||||||||||||bl||pl||||||||||||pl|bl||||pl|pl|pl|rl|nl||ql|kl||nl|rl| |responses=
*[[/5...d5|5...d5 - Schlechter Defence]] *[[/5...Nf6|5...Nf6 - Classical Defence]] *[[/5...Bb4|5...Bb4+ - Copenhagen Defence]] *[[/5...Nc6|5...Nc6 - to Göring Gambit]] *[[/5...d6|5...d6 - the 5...d6 Defence]] |}} = Danish Gambit Accepted = The pawn is recaptured. White has great attacking chances with her two open bishops and quick development, but Black is up two pawns. A player who is up two pawns can safely assume that they're going to win any endgame that arises, which means White's attack needs concrete results - either material, or checkmate. Rather than accept those stakes, Black often gambits a pawn straight back with [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...d5|'''5...d5''']] to get her queen and c8-bishop into the game. This is the Schlechter Defence, in which Black can either try to hold onto the second pawn, or return that one too to steer the game into a level, queenless middlegame. A more ambitious approach is [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6|'''5...Nf6''']], the Classical Defence. It looks like the knight is just walking into an e5 advance, but tactical considerations mean it's not that simple. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Bb4|'''5...Bb4+''']] is the Copenhagen Defence. Committing the bishop to b4 invites a later Qb3, but who doesn't love developing a piece with check when you're behind in development? [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...d6|'''5...d6''']] is not fatal, but abandons any hope of active defence in favour of Turtle Mode. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nc6|'''5...Nc6''']] offers a transposition to the Göring Gambit. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...c6|'''5...c6''']] hampers the b8-knight and doesn't actually help Black achieve ...d5. Likewise 5...Qe7 and 5...f6 are anti-developing moves, and the attempted Scholar's Mate with 5...Qh4 doesn't work. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Bc4 cxb2 5. Bxb2''' {| cellpadding="4" cellspacing="0" border="0" ! ! align="left" |5 !6 ! align="left" |7 !8 | |- ! align="right" |Schlechter Defense |... d5 |Bxd5 Nf6 |Bxf7+ Kxf7 |Qxd8 Bb4+ |= |} {{wikipedia|Danish Gambit}}{{ChessMid}}{{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

{{Chess Opening  Theory/Position|Danish Gambit  Accepted||rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd||rd|pd|pd|pd|pd||pd|pd|pd||||||nd|||||||||||||bl||pl||||||||||||pl|bl||||pl|pl|pl|rl|nl||ql|kl||nl|rl||}}

= Danish Gambit Accepted, Classical Defence =

=== 5...Nf6 ===
Black's knight on f6 is targeting the undefended e-pawn. Turning the tables with '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6/6. e5|6. e5]]''' is an obvious and strong choice.

Defending the pawn with '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6/6. Nc3|6. Nc3]]''' or, if you don't want to block the bishop's diagonal, with '''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6/6. Nd2|6. Nd2]]''' are less popular.  Although developing pieces can't be bad, if Black finds the accurate ...d5 in response then the pawn is getting blown up anyway.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6/6. Nf3|6. Nf3]]''' is just a bit too normal to be an optimal move in this crazy line. The moves Black needs to find in response are correspondingly quite normal ones, like castling kingside.

'''[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Bc4/4...cxb2/5. Bxb2/5...Nf6/6. Qb3|6. Qb3]]''' is obviously devastating if Black were forced to capture on e4, which she isn't. The immediate tactical problem for White is that 6...d5! now can't be met with 7.e5, because the White queen would find herself badly placed after 7...dxc4 8.exf6. 

The "forcing" 6. Bxf6 is a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad move. Apart from giving up the bishop pair, the Black queen that appears on f6 will target a1 (forcing the passive 7.Nd2) and also f2 in combination with a bishop on c5.

'''<big>6.e5</big>''' is the most popular and strongest move for White.{{ChessMid}}{{Chess Opening  Theory/Footer}}

= Danish Gambit Accepted, Classical  Defence =

=== 6. Nf3 ===
'''[[/6...Nxe4|6…Nxe4]]?'''  would be a great move to teach chess students about the value of development  over pawn-grabbing. The simple 7. O-O sets in motion an overwhelming  attack.

Part of the reason White wants to play 7. O-O is that it deprives Black of  the bishop check on b4, which is otherwise a free developing move. So it  makes sense that Black's most popular move is the immediate  '''[[/6...Bb4|6...Bb4+]]''' followed by castling, and that a less popular but  higher-scoring alternative is '''[[/6...d5|6...d5]]''' to distract White from  castling by threatening a piece. After 6...d5 7.exd5 Black has the nice d6  square for the bishop, Open Ruy Lopez style.

Black can opt for passive defence with '''[[/6...Be7|6...Be7]]''' or  '''[[/6...d6|6...d6]]''', or for a transposition to the Göring Gambit with  '''[[/6...Nc6|6...Nc6]]'''.

= Danish Gambit Accepted, Classical Defence =

=== 7. exf6 ===
Black will lose castling rights and have to play around a protected White pawn on g7 if she captures on c4 immediately.

So instead she throws in '''[[/7...Bb4|7...Bb4+]]'''. In responding to the check, White must either give up the dark-squared bishop, block the  dark-squared bishop's diagonal, block the d-file, or forfeit castling rights herself. All of those are good things for Black!

= Danish Gambit Accepted, Classical Defence =

=== 7...Bb4 ===
White has five legal moves to respond to the check. Ke2 is not the right one.

'''[[/8. Kf1|8. Kf1]]''' is surprisingly popular, but the positive of  keeping lines open is outweighed by the negative of losing castling rights,  especially since the h1-rook can't get out via h3 while Black's unopposed light-squared bishop is watching it.

'''[[/8. Nc3|8. Nc3]]''' looks natural, but 8...Qxf6! is a very cold shower. Far from stepping into a discovered attack, Black is setting up a devastating  cross-pin on the knight that White must waste several moves wriggling out of.

'''[[/8. Nd2|8. Nd2]]''' means it's White, not Black, who will lose castling rights after 8...dxc4. Thanks to the threatened pawn fork on c3,  White won't have time to reinforce d2 with Ngf3.

So by a process of elimination we have '''[[/8. Bc3|8. Bc3]]'''. This time there's a tactical flaw with 8...Qxf6, so Black must exchange bishops on c3 so as not to lose a piece.

=== 10...Rg8 ===
Black  is now threatening to trade queens on d1 with a winning advantage, as once the rook has captured on g7, White's Nd5 doesn't come with the threat of a fork on  f6, so Black can simply defend c7 with ...Na6.

So to limit the damage, White's queen usually makes tracks, with either  '''[[/11. Qf3|11. Qf3]]''' or '''[[/11. Qa4|11. Qa4+]]'''.

Another possibility is for White to voluntarily get the queens off with  '''[[/11. Qxd8|11. Qxd8+]]''', followed by castling queenside, hoping that an  all-out attack on Black's still underdeveloped forces will be enough  compensation for the two pawns.

Bxf6+ and White wins an exchange) Black has an advantage as he is still up a pawn and has the bishop pair, but accurate play is needed. Note that 6. exd5?! is inaccurate because the bishop on c4 is now blocked by its own pawn. == 4.Nxc3 ==
This move was Alekhine's choice. This move regains the one of the lost pawns, thus keeping White's material deficit to a minimum. White now has a huge lead in development and a central pawn.
